curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: `q{register}…q`; `@{register}`; `@@`; counts such as `10@a`; append with `qA`; inspect, put, and edit macro text; stable anchors over irregular rows; deliberate final cursor position; stopping on failed motion/search; recognizing when a macro is the wrong tool; optional recursion
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Record a robust transformation, replay it safely, inspect or repair it, state the assumptions that make it valid, and recognize the uniform case where a smaller tool wins
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Comment irregular calls; restructure repeated object entries; record on one row and apply to selected instances; repair a macro with a bad final motion; let a malformed row stop a counted replay
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core automation. Recursive macros are optional and never required for normal progression

reference.purpose: Record Normal-mode keys into a named register.
notes: Whatever movement the recording ends with becomes part of its contract.

reference.purpose: Replay a named macro or the latest replayed macro.
notes: Replay starts at the current cursor.

reference.purpose: Repeat a self-advancing macro a trusted number of times.
notes: A failed anchor stops the run and cancels the replays still owed.
A generous count is safe when the macro finds its own next target.

reference.command: line edges, finds, searches, text objects, %
reference.purpose: Build macro steps around durable textual structure.
notes: Rows that differ in width, depth, or nesting are what anchors are for.
A text object states what structure must exist; a character count does not.

reference.purpose: Choose where the next replay begins.
notes: Record movement only when every replay should advance.
An edit that adds or removes a row changes how far the ending must move.

reference.purpose: Append keys to register a without replacing it.
notes: Inspect before extending an unfamiliar macro.
Appended keys run as they are recorded, so the cursor moves with them.

reference.purpose: Put macro text, edit it, and write it back.
notes: Practice uses command-only macros so every key is readable.
Any yanked line of commands can be replayed as a macro.

reference.command: macro vs substitution vs ranged Normal
reference.purpose: Reserve macros for multi-step edits over rows that differ.
notes: Uniform adjacent rows belong to a substitution or, in Unit 14, a ranged Normal command.
Search-selected replay is for instances that deserve a decision each time.

reference.purpose: Allow a macro to invoke a macro, including itself.
notes: Optional and never required for normal progression.
Prefer counted or search-selected replay while learning.

coverage.concept: stop on failed motion or search
inspect put and repair macro text
selective macro application and tool choice

lessons.title: Record once, replay deliberately
lessons.objective: Record a complete transformation in a named register and replay it safely.

activities.title: Record and replay a macro
activities.body: Press `q` and a register letter to start recording Normal-mode keys. Press `q` again to stop, then press `@` and that letter to replay the recorded keys. Record the movement to the next target too, and one replay becomes many.
activities.contrast: A macro stores keys and their assumptions, not an abstract refactor.

activities.title: Silence three queued calls
activities.instruction: Comment out the three queued calls at the top of the boot sequence, without touching the rest of the file.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Stop recording; register a now holds the edit and the move to the next row.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Replay it once more on the third call.

checkpoints.caption: One row is commented and the cursor already sits on the next target.
Three rows changed from one recording.

hints: Decide which row the recording should end on before pressing q the second time.
The comment marker belongs at the first nonblank character, not at column zero.
A recorded downward move makes every replay land on the next call.

feedback.success: Three calls are commented from a single recording.
feedback.why: The recording ended one row below its edit, so each replay started where the previous one finished.
feedback.contrast: Without that recorded move, every replay would edit the same row again.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript shows a call sequence whose rows a recorded comment edit can walk.

activities.title: Comment queued jobs
activities.instruction: Disable the four queued jobs with a comment marker, leaving the reporting calls below them alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.

hints: Record the edit and the move to the next job in one pass.
Stop recording only once the cursor has reached the following row.
Three replays finish the remaining jobs.

feedback.success: The four queued jobs are commented and the reporting calls are untouched.
feedback.why: A self-advancing recording turns one edit into four without repositioning by hand.
feedback.contrast: Replaying a recording that does not move would comment the first job four times.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: python keeps the comment marker short so the recording stays readable.

activities.title: Disable settings at two depths
activities.instruction: Comment out the three port entries and the debug flag below them, and mark each disabled row with a trailing “(off)”.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Enter Insert mode after the last character.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Replay on the third port entry.
Replay on the debug flag, two levels shallower.

checkpoints.caption: The last row sits at a different depth and still lands correctly.

hints: Both halves of the edit belong in one recording: the marker in front and the note behind.
Anchoring the comment marker to the first nonblank character survives the change of depth.
The final row is indented two spaces instead of four; the same recording still fits it.

feedback.success: Four rows are disabled and annotated, across two indentation depths.
feedback.why: Both edits anchored to the line's own structure rather than to a column number.
feedback.contrast: A recording that inserted at column zero would have broken the indentation on every row.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: yaml nests keys at different depths, so the recording cannot assume a column.

activities.title: Mute a statement batch
activities.instruction: Comment out the whole audit, insert, and count batch between the first update and the trailing update, so only the surviving statements run.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.

hints: Six rows change and they alternate between two indentation depths.

feedback.success: The six statement rows are commented and the trailing update still runs.
feedback.why: One recording covered both statement heads and their indented continuation rows.
feedback.contrast: Stopping at the wrong row would have left a continuation row running without its statement.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: sql wraps continuation rows at a deeper indent than their statement heads.

activities.title: Choose the smaller repeat tool
activities.prompt: Ten adjacent, identically shaped rows each need the same short change, and the cursor lands on the next row with a single `j`. What should you reach for?

options.label: Move with `j`, then repeat the change with `.`
Record a macro that moves and repeats the change
A Visual Block change across the rows

activities.explanation: A single known motion between identical rows is dot-repeat's own case; recording adds register management for a sequence `.` already replays, and Visual Block assumes the change sits in the same column on every row, which uniform row shape alone does not guarantee.

lessons.title: Replay at useful scale
lessons.objective: Use @@ and counts to repeat the latest macro without losing control.

activities.title: Repeat the latest macro or run it several times
activities.body: Press `@@` to replay the last macro again. Add a count, as in `10@a`, to run register `a` ten times. A macro that searches for its own next target can cross rows that do not need the edit.
activities.contrast: Counts are fast when every instance is trusted; separate replays are easier to inspect.

activities.title: Flag scattered warnings
activities.instruction: Mark every warning row in the log with a leading “! ”, leaving the information rows between them alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the next row that begins with the warning tag.
Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Stop recording; the search is part of the macro.
Replay the macro stored in register a.

checkpoints.caption: The recording found its own target before editing it.
Three warnings marked; the information rows never moved.

hints: The search belongs inside the recording, before the edit.
The marker changes the start of the row, so the same search cannot find it twice.
The second replay can reuse the latest macro instead of naming the register again.

feedback.success: All three warnings carry the marker and nothing else changed.
feedback.why: Searching first means the macro locates its next target instead of assuming the next row.
feedback.contrast: A recording that stepped down one row would have marked information rows instead.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows put the interesting lines at unpredictable distances from each other.

activities.title: Continue the latest list macro
activities.instruction: Replace the tag on each outstanding item with an unchecked task box, leaving the notes between them as prose.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the next outstanding item.
Delete the tag word at the start of the row.
Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Replay the macro stored in register a.

hints: Let the recording find its own next item rather than counting rows.
Removing the tag changes how the row starts, which keeps the search moving forward.
The last application can reuse the latest macro.

feedback.success: Three items became task boxes and the prose rows are untouched.
feedback.why: A search-led recording skips whatever sits between two matches.
feedback.contrast: Stepping down a fixed number of rows would have boxed a sentence instead.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: markdown mixes prose and list rows, so the targets are not adjacent.

activities.title: Retire the legacy helpers
activities.instruction: Mark the definition row of every legacy helper with a trailing “# legacy” note, leaving the current helpers alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the next legacy definition.
Enter Insert mode after the last character.
Run the macro three more times, once per remaining legacy helper.

hints: Count the legacy definitions before choosing a number.
The recording should find its own next target so the count can be trusted.
Three helpers remain after the recorded one.

feedback.success: Four legacy definitions carry the note and every current helper is intact.
feedback.why: Because the macro searched for its next target, a count could cross the helpers in between.
feedback.contrast: The same count on a row-stepping macro would have commented four consecutive rows.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: python definition rows start at column zero, so a search anchored to the line start is exact.

activities.title: Confirm every record in the export
activities.instruction: Append a trailing “,ok” to all thirteen record rows, including the ones below the visible window, and leave the region headings unchanged.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the next record row.
Enter Insert mode after the last field.
Run the macro once for every remaining record row.

hints: Thirteen rows need the field and one of them is already done by the recording.

feedback.success: Every record row ends with the confirmation field and the region headings are untouched.
feedback.why: The end-of-line anchor ignored the differing field counts, and the search stepped over each heading.
feedback.contrast: Twelve separate replays would have done the same work; the count is what makes recording worth it.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: csv records vary in field count, so only an end-of-line anchor fits every row.

activities.title: Choose the ranged command over the count
activities.prompt: The same short Normal-mode edit must run on lines 8 through 20, and that exact range is already known. What is the more direct tool?

options.label: Record the edit, then replay it with `12@a`
Manually redo the edit on each line

activities.explanation: A known, contiguous line range and a single Normal-mode edit is exactly what a ranged `:normal` states in one line; a recorded macro adds a recording step and a register for the same guaranteed range, and repeating the edit by hand discards the range entirely.

lessons.title: Anchor macros to structure
lessons.objective: Use textual structure instead of fragile absolute columns.

activities.title: Use structure instead of fixed columns in a macro
activities.body: Every macro step should name the structure it depends on: a line edge, the first nonblank character, a delimiter, a search, a text object, or a matching bracket. Ask which of those still holds when the next row has a different shape.
activities.grammar: line edge · delimiter · search · text object · matching bracket
activities.contrast: 8l assumes a width. A text object states what structure must exist, and fails loudly when it does not.

activities.title: Empty four call argument lists
activities.instruction: Clear the arguments of the first four calls, including the ones whose arguments are themselves wrapped in a call.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the first opening parenthesis on the row.
Delete everything inside that pair of parentheses.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Replay on the third call, whose argument is wrapped.

checkpoints.caption: A wrapped argument disappears with the rest, because the text object owns the whole pair.

hints: Find the opening parenthesis first, then let a text object decide how much to delete.
The parentheses pair is the structure; the number of characters between them is not.
Every row keeps its own call name and semicolon.

feedback.success: Four calls now have empty argument lists, wrappers included.
feedback.why: The delete named a pair of parentheses, so it matched however much text sat between them.
feedback.contrast: A counted delete tuned to the first row would have cut too little on the wrapped rows.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript nests calls inside calls, which is where a counted delete would fail.

activities.title: Restyle the nested backlog bullets
activities.instruction: Change the bullet character on the first four backlog rows to an asterisk, keeping every row's indentation exactly as it is.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the first nonblank character.
Replace the character under the cursor with an asterisk.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Run the macro three more times, once per remaining row.

hints: The bullet is the first nonblank character, whatever column it happens to occupy.
The first column and the first nonblank character are different anchors here.
Three rows remain after the recorded one.

feedback.success: Four bullets changed and every indentation level survived.
feedback.why: Anchoring to the first nonblank character made the differing depths irrelevant.
feedback.contrast: Replacing the character in the first column would have eaten the indentation on the nested rows.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: markdown nests list rows at several depths, so the bullet never sits in one column.

activities.title: Blank the checked-in secrets
activities.instruction: Replace the quoted value on the first three settings with TBD, whatever column the quotes start in.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the first quote on the row.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Replay on the third setting, which carries a trailing comment.

hints: The quotes start in a different column on each row, so find them rather than count to them.
A quoted text object replaces the value whatever its length.
The trailing comment on the last row must survive untouched.

feedback.success: Three secrets are blanked and the trailing comment is intact.
feedback.why: The quote pair, not a column, defined how much text the change replaced.
feedback.contrast: Changing a fixed number of characters would have left fragments of the longer values behind.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: php assignments put the quoted value at a different column on every row.

activities.title: Terminate the unfinished calls
activities.instruction: Put the missing semicolon directly after each unfinished call's closing parenthesis, ahead of any trailing comment.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the first opening parenthesis on the row.
Jump to the parenthesis that closes it.
Enter Insert mode after that character.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Run the macro three more times, once per remaining call.

hints: The closing parenthesis is not the last character on every row.

feedback.success: Four calls are terminated and each trailing comment still trails.
feedback.why: Matching the bracket found the true end of the call, even with nesting and a comment after it.
feedback.contrast: Appending at the line end would have pushed two semicolons into the middle of a comment.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: c rows mix nested calls with trailing comments, so the line end is the wrong place to edit.

lessons.title: Finish where the next replay begins
lessons.objective: Design the last motion as part of the macro's contract.

activities.title: Plan where a macro leaves the cursor
activities.body: A replay starts wherever the previous one stopped, so the last motion is part of the recording's contract. When the macro's first step is relative — a find, a word motion, a case flip — the ending has to restore the position that step assumes.
activities.contrast: Movement left outside the recording must be repeated by hand before every replay.

activities.title: Convert three settings to assignments
activities.instruction: Turn the colon into an equals sign on the three server settings, so each replay still starts where the find can work.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator on the row.
Replace it with an equals sign.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Return to the first column, so the next find starts from the row's edge.
Replay the macro stored in register a.

checkpoints.caption: The cursor is back at a column every row has.
Three settings converted; the section headings never matched the find.

hints: The recording ends at the column where the next replay will begin.
The separator sits at column fourteen on the first row and column four on the next one.
Returning to the row's edge costs one key and makes every replay safe.

feedback.success: Three settings are assignments and the recording can still run again.
feedback.why: The recorded ending returned to the first column, so the find had the whole row to search.
feedback.contrast: Ending one row down but fourteen columns in would have left the find nothing to reach on a shorter row.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: toml keys differ enough in length that a carried-over column breaks the next find.

activities.title: Export the leading struct fields
activities.instruction: Capitalize the first letter of the first four struct fields, leaving their indentation and the fields below them alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Flip the case of the character under the cursor.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Move to the first nonblank character of that row.
Run the macro three more times, once per remaining field.

hints: The case flip works on the character under the cursor, so the ending decides which character that is.
Every row is indented; the first column is a space, not a letter.
Three fields remain after the recorded one.

feedback.success: Four fields are exported and their indentation is unchanged.
feedback.why: Ending at the first nonblank character put the cursor on a letter before every replay.
feedback.contrast: Ending at the first column would have flipped the case of a space and left the field unexported.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: go struct fields are indented, so the first column holds whitespace rather than the letter.

activities.title: Split the doubled-up commands
activities.instruction: Break the first three doubled-up commands into one command per row, and finish ready for the next doubled row rather than the half you just created.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator between the two commands.
Replace it with a line break.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Replay on the third doubled row.

hints: The split leaves the cursor on the row it just created, not on the next doubled row.
Count the rows the buffer gains before deciding how far the ending should move.
Each replay has to reach the next doubled row, not the row the split just created.

feedback.success: Three doubled rows became six single commands and the rest of the script is unchanged.
feedback.why: The edit added a row, and the recorded ending stepped past it onto the next target.
feedback.contrast: An ending that moved two rows down would have skipped a doubled row every time.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: shell rows often chain two commands, and splitting one adds a row the macro has to account for.

activities.title: Escalate the first four errors
activities.instruction: Mark the first four error rows with a leading “! ”, finishing on the fifth so the remaining error is ready to review.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
End the recording on the next error row.
Run the macro three more times, once per remaining error.

hints: The ending is not a row movement here; the next target is a search away.

feedback.success: Four errors are marked and the cursor waits on the fifth.
feedback.why: Because the marker changes how a row starts, the recorded search always moved on to an unmarked error.
feedback.contrast: A recorded downward step would have marked information rows, and a search recorded first would have skipped the error under the cursor.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows put errors at unpredictable distances, so the ending cannot be a fixed number of rows.

activities.title: Choose the macro for irregular structure
activities.prompt: Several scattered lines need the same multi-step edit, but each line's target field sits in a different position relative to its neighbors. What should you reach for?

options.label: A macro anchored by search, replayed per match
A `:global` command running one Normal sequence
A single dot-repeat with a count

activities.explanation: Differing local structure is what a macro's own search anchors are built to absorb; `:global` assumes the same Normal sequence works unchanged on every matched line, and a counted dot-repeat assumes uniform adjacent rows — neither holds for this irregular case.

lessons.title: Let broken assumptions stop replay
lessons.objective: Use failed motions and searches as safe stopping conditions.

activities.title: A failed motion stops the macro
activities.body: When a recorded find or search cannot reach its target, Vim stops that run and cancels the replays still owed to a count. That is a feature: the row that broke the macro's assumption is left exactly as it was, and so is everything after it.
activities.grammar: anchor fails → macro stops · remaining count cancelled
activities.contrast: A motion that still succeeds in the wrong place is far more dangerous than one that fails.

activities.title: Stop at the malformed contact
activities.instruction: Convert the separators in the contact list to equals signs, and let the malformed row below the window end the run before it reaches the rows underneath.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator on the row.
Replace it with an equals sign.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Ask for nine more runs, one for every remaining contact row.

checkpoints.caption: Six replays ran, the seventh found no separator, and the two owed after it never started.

hints: The count says how many runs you want, not how many the buffer can support.
One row below the window has no separator at all.
The run that cannot find its anchor stops, and the rows after it stay untouched.

feedback.success: Seven rows converted and the macro stopped itself at the malformed row.
feedback.why: The find had nothing to reach on that row, so Vim ended the run and cancelled the replays still owed.
feedback.contrast: A macro anchored to a column would have replaced whatever character happened to sit there.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: csharp resource rows are uniform enough that the one malformed row is the only thing a macro can trip on.

activities.title: Stop before the broken log row
activities.instruction: Replace the first separator on each log row with a comma, and stop where a row without a separator makes the run unsafe.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator on the row.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Ask for eight more runs and let the buffer decide how many happen.

hints: One row in the middle carries no separator.
The count can be larger than the number of rows that qualify.
Nothing below the broken row should change.

feedback.success: Five rows carry commas and the run ended at the row without a separator.
feedback.why: A failed find is the macro's stopping condition, so the rows after it were never touched.
feedback.contrast: Repeating the edit by hand would have needed a decision at every row instead of one at the end.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows share a pipe layout, so a row missing it is a genuine defect rather than a variant.

activities.title: Stop when the search runs out
activities.instruction: Comment out the indented debug prints, and let the run end by itself once no debug print is left rather than counting them first.

commandGroups.explanation: Jump to the next indented debug print.
Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Ask for seven more runs without counting the prints first.

hints: The recording finds its own target, so the search is what eventually fails.
A generous count is safe here: the extra runs have nothing to find.
Commenting a row changes how it starts, which is why the search keeps moving forward.

feedback.success: All four debug prints are commented and the extra runs stopped harmlessly.
feedback.why: Once no row matched the search any more, the run ended and the remaining count was cancelled.
feedback.contrast: A row-stepping macro with the same count would have commented working code.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: python indents its debug calls, so an anchored search can name them precisely.

activities.title: Cancel the remaining counted replays
activities.instruction: Drop the trailing field from each export record, and let the single-field row deep in the file cancel whatever replays are still owed.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the last character of the row.
Find the last separator, searching backwards.
Delete from the separator to the end of the row.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Ask for fourteen more runs and let the record without a separator end them.

hints: Records carry two to four fields, so the last separator is not in a fixed column.

feedback.success: Eleven records lost their trailing field and the single-field record stopped the run.
feedback.why: Searching backwards from the row end found the last separator whatever the field count, and its failure was the guard.
feedback.contrast: A forward find would have cut every record after its first field instead.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: csv records differ in field count, so only a backward find from the row end reaches the last separator.

lessons.title: Extend a useful recording
lessons.objective: Append keys with an uppercase register instead of rerecording from scratch.

activities.title: Add more keys to an existing macro
activities.body: Lowercase `qa` replaces register `a`; uppercase `qA` keeps what it holds and records onto the end of it. The appended keys run as you record them, so the cursor is already in position when you stop.
activities.contrast: Appending is safest after inspecting what the register already contains.

activities.title: Add the missing advance
activities.instruction: Repair the hyphenated names in the first four selected columns, starting from a recording that edits one row but never moves on.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the hyphen on the row.
Stop recording; the macro edits a row but stays on it.
Reopen register a and append to what it already holds.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Stop again; register a now ends with the advance.
Run the extended macro three times, once per remaining column.

checkpoints.caption: The register holds the edit only, so a replay would land on the same row.
The appended keys ran while being recorded, so the cursor already waits on the next column.

hints: The first recording is worth keeping; only its ending is missing.
An uppercase register name appends instead of replacing.
The keys you append also run, which is why the count starts from the next row.

feedback.success: Four column names use underscores, and register a now holds a self-advancing macro.
feedback.why: Appending kept the working edit and added the movement it lacked.
feedback.contrast: Rerecording from scratch would have discarded a correct edit to add one motion.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: sql column lists repeat one row shape, so the missing advance is the only defect in the recording.

activities.title: Extend a settings macro
activities.instruction: Turn the first four settings into assignments without their stray trailing semicolons, keeping the recording you already have.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator on the row.
Replace it with an equals sign.
Reopen register a and append to what it already holds.
Move to the last character of the row.
Delete the stray character under the cursor.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Run the extended macro three times, once per remaining setting.

hints: Keep the separator fix and add the second half to the same register.
The trailing character sits at the end of the row, whatever its length.
The advance belongs at the end of the appended keys, not before them.

feedback.success: Four settings are clean assignments and register a performs both repairs.
feedback.why: One append turned a partial recording into a complete, self-advancing one.
feedback.contrast: Two separate macros would have meant two passes over the same rows.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: shell environment files show both defects on one row: the wrong separator and a trailing character.

activities.title: Extend a quoting macro
activities.instruction: Give the first five keys the same double quotes the rest of the object uses, extending the recording that fixes only the opening quote.

commandGroups.explanation: Replace it with a double quote.
Reopen register a and append to what it already holds.
Repeat the find, which lands on the closing single quote.
Move one line down, inside the recording.
Run the extended macro four times, once per remaining key.

hints: The closing quote is the next match of the find you already recorded.
Repeating a find costs one key and stays anchored to the row's own text.
Four keys remain after the recorded one.

feedback.success: Five keys are double quoted and the entries below were already correct.
feedback.why: Appending a repeat of the find reused the anchor the recording had established.
feedback.contrast: A second find recorded from the row start would have landed on the opening quote again.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: json keys carry two quotes, so a recording that fixes one is visibly incomplete.

activities.title: Extend a macro across scattered rows
activities.instruction: Give the first four warning rows a colon separator, extending a recording that edits a row but cannot reach the next warning.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the separator on the row.
Reopen register a and append to what it already holds.
Append a jump to the next warning row.
Run the extended macro three times, once per remaining warning.

hints: The warnings are not adjacent, so the appended ending cannot be a row step.

feedback.success: Four warnings use the colon separator and the information rows are untouched.
feedback.why: The appended search made the recording self-advancing across rows that had to be skipped.
feedback.contrast: An appended downward step would have rewritten the information row directly below.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log rows interleave warnings with information rows, so the advance has to be a search rather than a step.

lessons.title: Treat a macro as editable text
lessons.objective: Put macro text into the buffer, repair it, and write it back to its register.

activities.title: A macro can be inspected as register text
activities.body: A register holds characters, so any line of keys can become a macro and any macro can become a line of text. Yank a command-only recipe into register `a` to run it, put register `a` into the buffer to read it, and edit that text when the recipe is wrong.
activities.contrast: Recorded Insert text carries control characters; these lessons repair command-only macros so every key stays readable.

activities.title: Run the runbook's recorded fix
activities.instruction: Apply the key sequence written at the top of the runbook to the four warning rows below it.

commandGroups.explanation: Yank the rest of the row into register a.
Run the yanked text as a macro, once per warning row.

checkpoints.caption: Register a now holds six ordinary characters.
Those characters ran as commands, four times over.

hints: The register does not care whether its characters arrived from a recording or from a yank.
Yank only the keys, not the newline, so the register stays characterwise.
The written sequence already ends by moving to the next row.

feedback.success: Four warning rows use commas, driven by text that was never recorded.
feedback.why: A macro is register content, so yanked characters replay exactly like recorded ones.
feedback.contrast: Retyping the sequence by hand on every row would have cost four times as many keys.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log runbooks often carry the fix as a written key sequence above the rows it repairs.

activities.title: Reveal what the register holds
activities.instruction: Show the contents of register a after the “check=” marker, so the recipe can be read before anyone runs it.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the last character of the marker row.
Put register a after the cursor.

hints: The register's contents can be read only once they are somewhere visible.
Putting after the last character keeps the marker intact.
Nothing else in the checklist should change.

feedback.success: The recipe is readable on the marker row and the checklist is untouched.
feedback.why: Putting a register into the buffer is the direct way to see what a macro would do.
feedback.contrast: Running an unfamiliar macro before reading it risks an edit nobody predicted.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: markdown keeps a checklist and its notes in one document, which is where a recipe row belongs.

activities.title: Repair a bad delimiter
activities.instruction: Correct the recipe row so it names the separator the entries actually use, then apply it to the first four entries.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the wrong delimiter in the recipe.
Replace it with the separator the entries use.
Yank the rest of the row into register a.
Run the repaired recipe once per entry.

hints: The recipe row is ordinary text, so the same editing commands work on it.
The register has to be reloaded after the text changes.
Four entries need the change and the recipe already advances.

feedback.success: The recipe names the right separator and four entries carry colons.
feedback.why: Editing the text and yanking it back replaced the register's contents in one step.
feedback.contrast: Rerecording the macro would have meant retyping keys that were already correct.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: python configuration entries use a semicolon here, which is exactly what the written recipe gets wrong.

activities.title: Repair a macro that cannot repeat
activities.instruction: Fix the ending of the recipe row so a counted run reaches every record, then convert the first five records.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the last character of the recipe.
Replace the ending with a return to the first column.
Yank the rest of the row into register a.
Run the repaired recipe once per record.

hints: The recipe's last key decides where the next run starts, and the row end is not a column every record shares.

feedback.success: Five records use semicolons and the recipe can now run as many times as it is asked to.
feedback.why: Only the final motion was wrong, so repairing one character made the whole macro repeatable.
feedback.contrast: Left as it was, the second run would have found no separator to the right of the cursor and stopped.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: csv records vary in width, which is what makes the recipe's line-end ending fail on the second run.

lessons.title: Apply macros only where they fit
lessons.objective: Choose instances deliberately, and say when a macro is not the right tool at all.

activities.title: Use search to choose where a macro runs
activities.body: Record one local edit with no movement of its own, then let search decide which rows receive it. Every replay is a separate decision, which is what you want when only some rows qualify.
activities.contrast: Uniform rows in one range do not need this: a substitution states the change once, and Unit 14's ranged Normal command covers the rest.

activities.title: Comment only the debug calls
activities.instruction: Comment out the first three debug calls, leaving the work calls between them running.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Stop recording; the macro edits a row and stays there.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Apply it to the third debug call.

checkpoints.caption: The recording has no movement of its own, so it cannot run away.
Three debug calls commented; every work call still runs.

hints: Keep the movement out of the recording when only some rows qualify.
Search picks the instances; the macro only performs the edit.
Commenting a row stops it matching, so the next match is always fresh work.

feedback.success: Three debug calls are commented and nothing else moved.
feedback.why: The macro carried the edit and the search carried the judgment about where it belonged.
feedback.contrast: A self-advancing macro would have commented the work calls sitting between them.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: javascript interleaves debug calls with the work they instrument, so only some rows qualify.

activities.title: Select the flagged review notes
activities.instruction: Mark the first three flagged notes with a leading exclamation mark, leaving the ordinary review lines alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Apply it to the third flagged note.

hints: The recording should do the edit and nothing else.
Search is what tells the macro which rows qualify.
The ordinary review lines must look exactly as they do now.

feedback.success: Three flagged notes carry the marker and the ordinary lines are untouched.
feedback.why: Separating the edit from the selection let each replay be its own decision.
feedback.contrast: A count would have been faster and would have marked the ordinary lines too.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: prose review notes mix flagged items with ordinary commentary, so the qualifying rows must be chosen.

activities.title: Mark only the error records
activities.instruction: Prefix the first four error records with a leading “! ”, including the ones below the visible window, and leave every other record alone.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Apply the latest macro to the fourth error record.

hints: Only the error records qualify; the warnings do not.
After the first replay, the latest macro can be reused without naming the register.
Two of the four error records sit below the window.

feedback.success: Four error records are marked, including the ones off screen, and the warnings are unchanged.
feedback.why: Search moved between qualifying rows while the macro repeated only the edit.
feedback.contrast: Marking every record with a count would have flagged routine rows as problems.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: log files bury a few error records among many routine ones, spread further than one window.

activities.title: Mute the selected updates
activities.instruction: Comment out the four update statements scattered through the migration, leaving every insert and select able to run.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter Insert mode at the first nonblank character.
Replay the macro stored in register a.
Apply it to the third update.
Apply it to the fourth update.

hints: Every third row qualifies, but the pattern that says so is the leading keyword, not the spacing.

feedback.success: Four updates are commented and every insert and select survives.
feedback.why: The search named the statement kind, so the macro never had to guess from position.
feedback.contrast: A macro that stepped three rows at a time would break the moment a statement is added.

activities.portability: Uses named-register macro behavior shared by Vim and conforming Vim integrations.

provenance.languageRationale: sql migrations mix statement kinds, so the qualifying rows are defined by their leading keyword.

activities.title: Choose the smallest safe automation
activities.prompt: Several nonadjacent rows need the same multi-step structural edit, and each row's fields sit at a different column. Which tool should you try first?
activities.explanation: The transformation is multi-step and its rows differ in shape, so a macro's anchors do the analysis; search selects the nonadjacent instances deliberately.

activities.title: Decide when not to record
activities.prompt: Twenty adjacent rows are identical in shape, and each needs the same word replaced with another. Which tool fits best?

options.label: A recorded macro with a count

activities.explanation: Uniform rows and a plain textual replacement are the substitution's own case: it states the change once and reports what it touched. Recording adds setup cost and a per-row failure mode for no benefit, and Unit 14's ranged Normal command covers the same ground when the edit is a Normal command rather than a pattern.

activities.title: Macros are tiny programs with contracts
activities.body: Record from a stable anchor, finish at a deliberate cursor position, replay only where the assumptions hold, and inspect the register when the program needs repair. A macro earns its keystrokes when the rows differ from each other; when they are uniform and adjacent, a substitution or a ranged Normal command is the better answer. Recursive macros exist, but they remain optional because safe ordinary replay is the core skill.
takeaways: qa…q records; @a replays; @@ repeats the latest macro.
Counts scale a trusted self-advancing macro; search selects rows a count would ruin.
qA appends, and register text can be put, edited, and yanked back.
A failed anchor stops replay and cancels the runs a count still owed.
Uniform adjacent rows are a substitution's case, not a macro's.
